title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti Twp halts power infrastructure for a major data center as local pushback grows statewide.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your daily podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Friday, August 21, and local boards are moving fast on data center rules while power demand keeps rising.
Our big story today is yesterday's unanimous vote in Ypsilanti Township.
Trustees approved a land-use moratorium aimed squarely at new electric infrastructure for data centers.
This directly hits a proposed University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory research facility at Textile and Bridge roads.
The 220,000-square-foot project would need major new power lines, and the township just blocked that path for now.
Graham, why does this moratorium matter beyond that one site?
It shows townships using zoning and infrastructure rules to regain local control instead of waiting for state action.
We've seen similar moves in other places recently.
Exactly. Yesterday a different Michigan township banned new power lines to stop its own hyperscale project.
And New Buffalo Township rejected a special land-use request after residents raised water and noise concerns.
Bay City neighbors packed a planning meeting to oppose proposals over electricity, water, and industrial noise.
So what's the bigger picture on power demand here?
Former congressman Mike Rogers told Detroit voters yesterday he supports a temporary halt on new data centers to avoid higher electric bills.
How would one big facility affect bills for people 30 miles away?
Utilities have said AI-driven demand is already straining grids, and adding large loads without limits could push rates up across the region.
What about water use?
Cooling systems in these centers can draw millions of gallons daily, which worries rural and suburban areas already managing their own supplies.
And farmland?
Many proposals sit on former agricultural land, so towns are weighing lost tax revenue from farms against potential data center payments.
Who are the main players in the Ypsilanti case?
The University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory are tied to the research center, while local residents and the township board are pushing back on infrastructure.
Is this the first time Ypsilanti Township has taken this kind of step?
It's part of a wave we've seen this week, with boards tightening rules on size, location, and utility connections rather than leaving it to state regulators.
What happens next for that specific project?
The moratorium limits major utility work, so the developers may need to revise plans or seek other routes, and more public hearings are likely.
How does this fit with the Saline Township news?
The backer there just bought the neighboring golf course, which residents see as a sign of bigger expansion and more power requests ahead.
And in Vevay Township today?
Landowners want to annex into the city of Mason to clear the way for a data center, shifting tax revenue and control from the township.
That could affect Lansing or Jackson residents too.
Yes, through added power and water demand if the project scales up.
Meanwhile Washtenaw County is expanding local oversight on multiple proposals.
The Sun Times News roundup shows boards moving ahead with tighter rules on size and location instead of waiting for Lansing.
Mundy Township in Genesee County is also seeing early interest in a former manufacturing site.
Officials are fielding questions about water draw and grid upgrades that could touch nearby property values.
So the pattern is clear: more communities are asking hard questions before projects advance.
And yesterday's moratorium in Ypsilanti is the latest example of that local-first approach.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
More township meetings on infrastructure bans, annexation votes, and possible developer responses to the new limits.
Thanks for laying that out, Graham.
Now let's move to quick hits on the other stories from the last day.
Rogers' call for a temporary halt got attention in Detroit.
He linked it directly to avoiding higher power costs from AI projects.
The OpenAI-Oracle developer also bought a golf course next to its planned Michigan campus.
That signals possible expansion despite local concerns about footprint and grid pull.
And the Saline backer did the same thing with its own neighboring course.
Residents there are watching for bigger tax-break requests down the line.
New Buffalo Township turned down the special land-use request after hearing from residents.
The denial keeps that southwest Michigan project on hold for now.
Bay City residents turned out in force at the planning commission.
They flagged heavy electricity and water demands plus noise that could reach homes.
Mundy Township is getting early inquiries on that old manufacturing parcel.
Genesee County officials are fielding questions on water and upgrades.
Vevay Township landowners are pushing for annexation into Mason today.
That would move tax revenue and control to the city for the data center path.
Washtenaw County oversight is expanding on multiple proposals per the weekly roundup.
Boards there are setting their own size and location rules.
And the Rogers comments came just as utilities warn about grid strain.
All of it points to rising local pushback this week.
Let's check what's on deck for listeners who want to attend meetings.
No major data center-related meetings are listed on public agendas for the weekend.
We'll keep watching township boards and planning commissions as new items drop.
Residents should check their local clerk's office or websites for updates.
That wraps our look at the latest developments.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening.

episode_title: Ypsilanti Twp Moratorium Targets Power Lines for U-M Data Center Project
